messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Auditory (Babies): Babies
  Maladaptive Strategies: Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Vignette:
Mariam was 34, a divorced Middle Eastern woman who had spent the past several years working long days in agricultural fields, rising before dawn with other laborers and moving between rows of crops for much of the week. The trauma she described had not happened to her in the sense of direct physical injury, but she had witnessed it closely enough that it still felt to her as though she had been standing inside it. During a shift in a crowded packing area, she saw a young woman collapse after a sudden confrontation and the desperate attempts of bystanders to help. Mariam could still picture the confusion of voices, the sharp movement of bodies, and the helplessness of watching an ordinary workday turn frightening and chaotic in a matter of seconds. In the weeks afterward, she found that ordinary moments could bring the whole scene back with unsettling force. If someone nearby seemed suspiciously watchful or too focused on her, she would tense and scan their hands and face, certain that something was not right. Certain conversation topics also became difficult to tolerate, especially anything that drifted toward sudden illness, emergency response, or other distressing events; when coworkers began talking that way during breaks, she would go quiet, stare down at her gloves, and wait for the discussion to end. The sound of babies crying or fussing was another sharp reminder that caught her off guard. In a grocery store, a neighbor’s infant crying in the next aisle could make her chest tighten and her thoughts jump back to the helplessness she had felt hearing screams and frantic voices at the scene.

As the months passed, Mariam developed habits that made sense to her as ways of staying in control, even if they left her exhausted. After work she would clean and organize her small apartment repeatedly, wiping counters, straightening items on shelves, and checking that everything was in its proper place until the apartment felt temporarily manageable. She told herself that if the outside world was unpredictable, at least her home did not have to be. When distressing images or thoughts came back to her, she tried to force them away immediately, pressing her lips together and pushing herself toward only positive thoughts, as if any admission of fear would make the memory stronger. She would repeat to herself that she should be grateful, that things could be worse, that she needed to stay hopeful. Yet the effort to keep those thoughts out never lasted long, and when they returned she experienced them as intrusive and unwelcome, something she had to fight off again and again.

Over time, Mariam became increasingly convinced that people were not what they seemed. The memory of confusion at the packing area had left her watching others with a caution that bordered on certainty, and she had come to believe that trust was dangerous. Coworkers who laughed too loudly or spoke in low tones across the field could seem secretive to her, and she often interpreted uncertainty in other people’s behavior as a sign that she was missing something important. She also felt that she no longer belonged anywhere. After her divorce, she had already felt somewhat suspended between households and communities, but now that sense of being out of place deepened into something more painful. At work she kept to herself more than before, avoiding casual conversation because she did not want to risk hearing the wrong topic or seeming too exposed. At home, the repeated cleaning and attempts to think positively left little room for rest or pleasure, and her evenings narrowed into routines that felt safer but lonelier.

By the time she sought help, Mariam’s symptoms had become difficult to dismiss. Her PCL-5 score reflected the intensity of what she was living with, but what brought her in was simpler: she was tired of feeling on guard in her own life. She said she wanted to stop bracing herself every time a baby cried nearby, every time a coworker looked at her too intently, every time a conversation veered toward something she might not be able to face. What frightened her most was the thought that she would go on like this indefinitely, mistrusting everyone, feeling as if she belonged nowhere, and having to work so hard each day just to keep her mind from going back to what she had seen.
